descriptors.definition: The valuation premise dictates whether a non-financial asset is measured on a standalone basis or in combination with other assets and liabilities. Combination valuation is mandated when market participants typically utilize the asset alongside complementary items to maximize its utility.
inclusion: intangible assets valued alongside supporting technological updates or rights
groups of complementary assets widely used together by market participants
exclusion: isolated valuations where combined use is not customary among market participants
nearby_distinctions: Differs from standalone asset valuation by bundling interdependent items together to reflect true economic synergy recognized by market participants.

descriptors.definition: Fair value measurement of liabilities and equity instruments assumes the item is transferred to a market participant at the measurement date while remaining outstanding. Entities must prioritize observable direct market prices and minimize unobservable inputs.
inclusion: financial and non-financial liabilities
entity equity instruments issued as business combination consideration
exclusion: extinguishment or settlement values that diverge from transfer assumptions
nearby_distinctions: Unlike asset valuation which measures items held, liability and equity valuation measures the price required to transfer an existing obligation or claim to a third party.

descriptors.definition: When direct quoted prices for liabilities or equity instruments are absent, an entity utilizes the quoted price of an identical item held by another party as an asset. If such asset prices are unavailable, the entity applies other observable inputs or accepted valuation techniques.
terminology: held by other parties as assets
inclusion: quoted prices of identical items held by market participants as assets
income and market valuation approaches
exclusion: entity-specific settlement amounts ignoring market counterparty perspectives
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from instances where instruments are not held externally, shifting the metric from mirror-asset prices to direct issuer-side valuation techniques.

descriptors.definition: When a liability or equity instrument is not held by another party as an asset, fair value is determined using valuation techniques from the perspective of the market participant that owes the liability or issued the claim. This requires relying on active market quotes, observable inputs, or income and market approaches.
inclusion: issuer perspective valuation models
income approach metrics
market approach metrics
exclusion: mirror-asset prices from external holders when no such holders exist
nearby_distinctions: Differs from cases with external asset holders because valuation must be modeled strictly from the obligor or issuer standpoint without reference to counterparties' asset quotations.

descriptors.definition: An entity managing groups of financial assets and liabilities on a net risk exposure basis may apply an exception to measure fair value on a net long or net short position. This permits pricing net risk exposures consistently with market participant practices for identical risk types and durations.
inclusion: groups of derivatives and offsetting financial contracts managed on a net exposure basis
net counterparty credit risk and market risk evaluations
exclusion: netting disparate risk types such as combining interest rate risk with commodity price risk
combining positions with misaligned durations
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from individual gross asset and liability fair valuation by shifting the unit of account to a combined net risk portfolio when market practice supports it.

descriptors.definition: Initial transaction prices represent entry prices which may or may not equal fair value exit prices depending on transaction specifics. Factors such as related-party terms, duress, mismatched units of account, or different markets can cause initial transaction prices to diverge from fair value.
inclusion: exchange transactions where entry and exit prices coincide
adjustments for related party terms or forced selling conditions
exclusion: assumptions that transaction prices automatically equal fair value without evaluating contextual factors
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts the entry price paid or received at transaction inception with the exit price required for fair value measurement, highlighting conditions causing them to differ.

descriptors.definition: Valuation techniques estimate the price of an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date by maximizing observable inputs and minimizing unobservable inputs. Entities can select single or multiple approaches based on available data and appropriate professional judgment.
inclusion: market approach techniques utilizing comparable asset and liability pricing
income and discounted cash flow models when appropriate
exclusion: valuation approaches when active market quoted prices are directly available
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from direct active market quotes by serving as estimation mechanisms deployed only when direct identical quotes are missing or insufficient.

descriptors.definition: Valuation techniques must prioritize relevant observable inputs and minimize unobservable inputs to establish consistency and comparability. The overall classification of an asset or liability class depends on the level of input that holds significance on an overall basis.
inclusion: Exchange market closing prices
Dealer market bid and ask prices
Brokered market order matching
Principal to principal negotiated prices
exclusion: Arbitrary valuation without market corroboration
Inputs failing to reflect market participant risk assumptions
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from specific hierarchy levels by establishing the overarching principle of maximizing observable and minimizing unobservable data.

descriptors.definition: Level 1 inputs comprise unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities accessible at the measurement date. These prices supply the most reliable evidence of fair value and require no adjustment when available.
inclusion: Direct quoted prices from primary active stock exchanges
Identical financial instruments traded in multiple accessible active markets
exclusion: Quoted prices subjected to significant after-hour adjustments
Prices originating from inactive or restricted markets
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from Level 2 and Level 3 inputs by relying exclusively on direct, unadjusted active market quotations for identical items.

descriptors.definition: Level 2 inputs consist of observable data other than quoted prices included within Level 1, applicable directly or indirectly for the asset or liability. For items with specified contractual terms, these inputs must remain observable across substantially the full term.
inclusion: Quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets
Interest rates and yield curves observable at commonly quoted intervals
Market-corroborated inputs and entity credit standing adjustments
exclusion: Unadjusted active market quotes for identical items
Internal forecasts devoid of corroborating market data
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from Level 1 by using indirect or similar-asset pricing rather than direct identical quotes, and from Level 3 by remaining observable.

descriptors.definition: Level 3 inputs represent unobservable parameters utilized for fair value measurement when relevant observable inputs are absent due to little or no market activity. These inputs incorporate entity assumptions and risk adjustments that market participants would apply in pricing.
inclusion: Adjustments to non-binding consensus prices using uncorroborated internal data
Financial forecasts of cash flows developed using an entity's own data
exclusion: Directly observable market quotes
Yield curves and interest rates observable at standard intervals
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from Level 1 and Level 2 inputs by the complete absence of directly or indirectly observable market benchmarks, necessitating internal estimations and risk adjustments.

descriptors.definition: Entities must disclose valuation techniques, inputs, and the effects of measurements on financial performance to help users assess fair value determinations. A systematic hierarchy workflow directs fair value classification based on quote availability, adjustment requirements, and the presence of significant unobservable inputs.
inclusion: Quantitative information about significant unobservable inputs
Reconciliation of opening and closing Level 3 balances
Transfers between fair value hierarchy levels
exclusion: Omission of valuation processes and policies for recurring items
Failure to disclose sensitivity changes for unobservable parameters
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from mere recognition rules by focusing strictly on explanatory transparency, reconciliation, and qualitative or quantitative disclosures of measurement parameters.

descriptors.definition: Published corporate reports provide practical disclosures demonstrating how entities apply measurement techniques and accounting policies for fair value. These reporting extracts illustrate real-world execution of valuation governance within financial statements.
inclusion: Entity-specific accounting policy disclosures on fair value
Categorized financial statement presentation notes
exclusion: Hypothetical valuation models lacking corporate reporting backing
Unverified draft calculations
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from theoretical standard text by presenting empirical corporate reporting compliance and application examples.
source_ambiguities: The source text provides only a heading and bibliographic reference without substantive accounting rules or data.

descriptors.definition: The standard prescribes accounting treatment for inventories, specifically addressing cost determination, expense recognition, and write-downs to net realizable value. It provides guidance on measurement techniques and cost formulas.
inclusion: guidance for determining inventory cost
guidance for subsequent recognition as an expense
measurement techniques like standard cost and retail method
exclusion: financial instruments
biological assets related to agricultural activity
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes between general inventory accounting and specialized financial instrument or biological asset frameworks.

descriptors.definition: The standard applies to all inventories except financial instruments, biological assets at the point of harvest, and certain producer or broker-trader inventories measured at fair value. It outlines the boundaries of applicability for different asset classes.
inclusion: all general inventories
harvested agricultural produce after initial fair value recognition
exclusion: financial instruments under Ind AS 32 and Ind AS 109
biological assets under Ind AS 41
nearby_distinctions: Differentiates between standard inventories and scoped-out items such as financial instruments and biological assets.

descriptors.definition: Inventories comprise assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, in the process of production for such sale, or as materials to be consumed in production or service rendering. Net realisable value represents estimated selling price less estimated costs of completion and disposal.
inclusion: goods held for resale
finished goods and work in progress
materials and supplies awaiting production use
exclusion: costs to fulfill a contract accounted under Ind AS 115 that do not form inventories
secondary packing materials and publicity materials
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes between primary packing material included in inventory and secondary packing or publicity costs excluded from inventory.

descriptors.definition: Inventories must be measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Total cost comprises purchase costs, conversion costs, and other expenses incurred in bringing the items to their present location and condition.
terminology: lower of cost and net realisable value
inclusion: purchase price and import duties
transport and handling charges
direct and systematic allocation of production overheads
exclusion: trade discounts and rebates deducted from purchase price
taxes recoverable from taxing authorities
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes purchase price components from subsequent handling and conversion expenditures.

descriptors.definition: Inventory carrying amounts are recognized as an expense in the period when the related revenue is recognized or when write-downs and losses occur. Reversals of previous write-downs reduce the expense amount in the period they occur.
inclusion: carrying amount of sold inventory recognized as expense
losses and write-downs to net realisable value
allocations to other asset accounts like property, plant and equipment
exclusion: immediate direct expensing when allocated to self-constructed assets before depreciation
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes immediate expense recognition from capitalization into other asset accounts such as property, plant and equipment.

descriptors.definition: Financial statements must disclose accounting policies for inventory measurement, cost formulas, carrying amount breakdowns, and amounts recognized in profit or loss. Additional disclosures cover inventories carried at fair value less costs to sell and items pledged as security.
inclusion: cost formulas used
carrying amounts categorized by merchandise, supplies, materials, work in progress, and finished goods
write-down reversals and pledged assets
exclusion: unrelated non-inventory asset disclosures
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes classification-based disclosures from general accounting policy narratives.

descriptors.definition: Listed entities apply specific accounting policies where inventories are stated at the lower of cost and net realisable value determined on an item-by-item basis. Cost calculation methods vary by inventory type, utilizing options such as FIFO, moving weighted average, or full absorption cost.
inclusion: gold valued on FIFO basis
stores, spares, and raw materials valued on moving weighted average rate
work-in-progress and finished goods valued on full absorption cost
exclusion: unfixed gold prices yet to be determined with suppliers
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes between moving weighted average valuation for raw materials and full absorption costing for work-in-progress.

descriptors.definition: Ind AS 2 differs from AS 2 by explicitly covering subsequent expense recognition, excluding commodity broker-traders measured at fair value less costs to sell, and defining fair value distinctions. It also provides detailed guidelines for assessing net realisable value write-down reversals and requires consistent cost formulas.
inclusion: rules on write-down reversals
explicit fair value and net realisable value distinctions
mandatory consistent cost formulas for similar items
exclusion: provisions absent in older AS frameworks
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts Ind AS 2 write-down reversal allowances and fair value definitions with the lack of such provisions in AS 2.

descriptors.definition: The standard prescribes accounting principles for property, plant, and equipment to allow financial statement users to understand entity investments and changes therein. It applies universally unless another standard mandates alternative treatments or excludes specific assets like biological assets or mineral rights.
inclusion: Tangible items held for production, supply, rental, or administrative use expected to last over one period
PPE used to develop or maintain biological assets, exploration assets, and mineral reserves
exclusion: PPE classified as held for sale
Biological assets related to agricultural activity other than bearer plants
Exploration and evaluation assets
Mineral rights and non-regenerative reserves
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from investment property by applying the cost model for owned investment property under specific guidance
Distinguished from biological assets by excluding non-bearer living plants

descriptors.definition: The standard governs all property, plant, and equipment accounting practices unless separate standards dictate unique methods. It specifies broad exclusions while maintaining coverage for assets supporting excluded extractive or agricultural operations.
inclusion: Tangible assets applied in administrative, supply, or production functions extending past one accounting period
exclusion: Assets governed exclusively by alternate standards such as Ind AS 105 or Ind AS 41
nearby_distinctions: Separates general operational infrastructure from specialized extractive and biological resource properties

descriptors.definition: This section outlines fundamental measurement terms governing asset valuation, residual allocations, and impairment tracking under the standard. It defines calculations for determining current book values against recoverable economic worth.
inclusion: Valuation definitions including fair value, carrying value, and recoverable limits
exclusion: General operational rules or recognition thresholds not tied directly to valuation terms
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes fair value market participant pricing from entity-specific internal cash flow estimations

descriptors.definition: Property, plant, and equipment costs qualify for asset recognition only when future economic benefits are probable and the item's cost can be reliably measured. Entities evaluate all initial acquisition expenses and subsequent operational expenditures using these core criteria.
inclusion: Initial asset acquisition costs meeting probability and measurement tests
Stand-by and servicing equipment meeting asset definitions
exclusion: Spare parts and servicing tools failing asset criteria which default to inventory classification
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes capitalized equipment spares from routine inventory spares based on operational deployment and holding period

descriptors.definition: An asset item is capitalized if and only if future economic inflows are probable and historical costs can be calculated reliably. This threshold dictates initial balance sheet inclusion for both foundational acquisitions and subsequent enhancement outlays.
inclusion: Costs satisfying both the probability of economic benefits and reliable measurement conditions
exclusion: Expenditures failing either probability or measurement thresholds
nearby_distinctions: Separates capitalizable outlays from standard period operational expenses

descriptors.definition: Specialized spare parts and stand-by equipment are categorized as property, plant, and equipment when they satisfy the standard asset definition. Items failing this threshold are treated as ordinary inventory supplies.
inclusion: Servicing and standby items utilized over multiple periods alongside primary assets
exclusion: Routine replacement parts classified under standard inventory rules
nearby_distinctions: Differentiates major capital spares from routine operational consumables stored for quick turnover

descriptors.definition: The standard does not mandate a universal recognition unit, requiring professional judgment to establish what constitutes an individual property item. Individually immaterial assets like tools and dies may be aggregated to apply recognition principles collectively.
inclusion: Aggregated minor tools, moulds, and dies evaluated collectively under materiality judgment
exclusion: Standalone major assets evaluated on an individual component basis
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes collective asset pools for minor tools from individually distinct heavy machinery items

descriptors.definition: Assets acquired for safety or environmental reasons qualify for recognition because they enable entities to extract future economic benefits from related assets. Without these compliance enhancements, underlying production assets could not legally or safely operate.
inclusion: Safety and environmental installations required to unlock operational benefits from other assets
exclusion: Discretionary outlays not tied to regulatory necessity or operational enablement
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes compliance-driven asset enhancements from direct revenue-generating machinery

descriptors.definition: Subsequent expenditures that replace parts of an asset or execute major overhauls are capitalized if recognition criteria are met, alongside the derecognition of old component carrying values. Conversely, routine day-to-day servicing costs are expensed immediately as incurred.
inclusion: Costs of scheduled component replacements and major overhauls meeting recognition tests
exclusion: Day-to-day servicing, minor repairs, and consumable labor costs
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes long-interval capital overhauls from routine day-to-day maintenance charges routed through profit or loss

descriptors.definition: Qualifying items of property, plant, and equipment are initially recorded at historical cost upon acquisition or construction. Cost components include purchase prices, directly attributable preparation outlays, and initial dismantling obligations.
inclusion: Purchase prices, site preparation, delivery, installation, and asset dismantling provisions
exclusion: General administrative overheads and abnormal waste expenses
nearby_distinctions: Separates initial acquisition cost models from subsequent revaluation or depreciation measurements

descriptors.definition: Property, plant, and equipment items eligible for asset recognition must be quantified initially at their total cost base. This base encapsulates net purchase pricing, direct setup outlays, and future site restoration obligations.
inclusion: Net purchase outlays, import duties, handling fees, and professional installation charges
exclusion: Refundable taxes, trade discounts, and general overhead costs
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes initial cost capitalisation from later fair value adjustments

descriptors.definition: The asset cost baseline comprises purchase considerations, direct bringing-to-location expenses, and estimated dismantling provisions. For self-constructed assets, internal manufacturing profits and abnormal material wastage are strictly excluded from the capitalized total.
inclusion: Direct labor, material, and site preparation costs for self-constructed assets
exclusion: Abnormal amounts of wasted material or labor and internal manufacturing profits
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes standard construction outlays from abnormal inefficiencies excluded from asset values

descriptors.definition: The cost of property, plant, and equipment acquired under deferred payment terms is recorded at its cash price equivalent at the recognition date. The difference between the total payments and this cash price equivalent is recognized as interest expense over the credit period.
inclusion: Present value calculations of future installments using implicit interest rates
Recognition of interest expense over the credit period
exclusion: Nominal total payment amounts as initial asset cost
Immediate expensing of deferred payment financing differences
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard cash purchases by requiring present value discounting and interest separation

descriptors.definition: Entities must choose either the cost model or the revaluation model as an accounting policy and apply it consistently to an entire class of property, plant, and equipment. These alternative bases govern the subsequent carrying value of assets after initial recognition.
inclusion: Selection of uniform accounting policies across asset classes
Subsequent measurement using cost or fair value frameworks
exclusion: Applying mixed measurement models within the same asset class
Applying policies selectively to individual assets rather than classes
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from initial recognition rules by focusing on ongoing asset valuation and adjustments

descriptors.definition: Entities must select either the cost model or the revaluation model as an accounting policy for an entire class of property, plant and equipment. This policy choice dictates how asset values are adjusted subsequent to initial recognition.
inclusion: Entity policy choice between cost and revaluation models
Consistent application across asset classes
exclusion: Inconsistent application of models within a single asset category
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from initial recognition by governing ongoing measurement choices

descriptors.definition: Under the cost model, an item of property, plant, and equipment is carried at its historical cost less any accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses. This represents one of the two primary alternative measurement bases after recognition.
inclusion: Deduction of accumulated depreciation from original cost
Deduction of accumulated impairment losses from original cost
exclusion: Upward adjustments to fair value without explicit revaluation model adoption
Reflecting market value fluctuations directly in the carrying amount
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts with the revaluation model by prohibiting upward re-estimations of fair value

descriptors.definition: Under the revaluation model, an asset whose fair value can be measured reliably is carried at a revalued amount, representing its fair value at the date of revaluation less subsequent depreciation and impairment. Revaluations must be performed with sufficient regularity to prevent material divergence from fair value.
inclusion: Carrying assets at fair value minus subsequent depreciation and impairment
Periodic revaluations based on market volatility
exclusion: Applying revaluation selectively to isolated assets without including the whole class
Maintaining unadjusted historical costs when fair values differ materially
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from the cost model through its reliance on periodic fair value adjustments and market references

descriptors.definition: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life, recognized in profit or loss unless included in another asset's carrying amount. Significant components of an item with distinct useful lives or consumption patterns must be depreciated separately.
inclusion: Systematic allocation over useful life
Separate depreciation of significant asset components
Periodic review of residual values and useful lives
exclusion: Depreciating land with unlimited useful life
Omitting depreciation when market values increase
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from impairment as a routine allocation of cost rather than an unexpected loss in recoverable value

descriptors.definition: Items of property, plant, and equipment are evaluated for impairment using specific accounting standards to determine recoverable amounts and recognize losses. Third-party compensation for impaired or lost assets is accounted for as a separate economic event and recognized when receivable.
inclusion: Identification and measurement of impairment losses
Recognition of receivable third-party compensation in profit or loss
exclusion: Netting replacement asset costs directly against compensation proceeds
Deferring compensation recognition beyond the date it becomes receivable
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from depreciation by addressing sudden or structural reductions in recoverable value rather than systematic allocation

descriptors.definition: The carrying amount of an item of property, plant, and equipment must be derecognized upon disposal or when no future economic benefits are expected from its use or disposal. Gains or losses from derecognition are calculated as the difference between net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount, and are recognized in profit or loss.
inclusion: Derecognition upon asset disposal or loss of future economic benefits
Recognition of replacement part carrying amounts with simultaneous derecognition of replaced parts
exclusion: Classifying derecognition gains as revenue
Failing to derecognize replaced components when new parts are capitalized
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from impairment by representing complete removal from the balance sheet due to retirement, sale, or lack of benefits

descriptors.definition: The carrying amount of property, plant, and equipment is derecognized upon disposal or when no further economic benefits are expected. The resulting gain or loss is calculated as the difference between net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount, and is included in profit or loss.
inclusion: Determining disposal date based on control transfer principles
Calculating gain or loss via net proceeds versus carrying amount
exclusion: Treating derecognition gains as operational revenue
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from routine depreciation adjustments by permanently removing the asset base

descriptors.definition: Financial statements must disclose comprehensive details for each class of property, plant, and equipment, including measurement bases, depreciation methods, useful lives, and a complete reconciliation of beginning and ending carrying amounts. Additional disclosures cover title restrictions, pledged assets, and construction commitments.
inclusion: Reconciliation of beginning to ending carrying amounts showing additions, disposals, and depreciation
Disclosures regarding title restrictions and pledged security
exclusion: Omitting reconciliations for non-material asset categories without policy backing
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from primary recognition and measurement rules by focusing on transparency and financial statement disclosures

descriptors.definition: Entities must disclose measurement bases, depreciation methods, useful lives, and reconciliations of beginning and ending balances for each class of property, plant, and equipment. Additional required disclosures encompass title restrictions, security pledges, and contractual acquisition commitments.
inclusion: Disclosure of measurement bases and depreciation rates
Movement reconciliation including additions, disposals, and revaluations
exclusion: Excluding commitments or encumbrances from explanatory notes
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from measurement rules by providing qualitative and quantitative context to financial statement users

descriptors.definition: When property, plant, and equipment are carried at revalued amounts, entities must disclose the revaluation effective date, involvement of independent valuers, comparative cost model carrying amounts, and revaluation surplus movements. Additional recommended disclosures cover idle assets and fully depreciated items still in use.
inclusion: Effective date of revaluation
Comparison against cost model carrying amounts
Revaluation surplus movement disclosures
exclusion: Omitting restrictions on distribution of revaluation surplus balances
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard cost model disclosures by requiring specialized fair value and surplus tracking metrics

descriptors.definition: Entities are encouraged to voluntarily disclose supplementary asset details such as idle property, fully depreciated items still in use, and retired assets. These disclosures provide stakeholders with enhanced transparency regarding asset utilization and valuation differentials when using the cost model.
inclusion: Carrying amount of temporarily idle PPE
Gross carrying amount of fully depreciated PPE still in use
Carrying amount of PPE retired from active use not classified as held for sale
Fair value under cost model when materially different from carrying amount
exclusion: Mandatory core financial statement line-item recognitions
Assets already classified as held for sale under Ind AS 105
nearby_distinctions: Differs from mandatory disclosures by being explicitly optional rather than required by the standard.

descriptors.definition: This guidance applies to adjustments in existing dismantling, removal, and site restoration obligations initially incorporated into the cost of property, plant and equipment or right-of-use assets. It governs how entities account for subsequent shifts in estimated cash outflows, discount rates, and the unwinding of the discount over time.
inclusion: Obligations recognized as part of PPE or right-of-use asset costs
Liabilities recognized under Ind AS 37
exclusion: Initial recognition estimates of decommissioning obligations
Liabilities outside the scope of asset cost capitalization
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from initial recognition by focusing exclusively on subsequent re-measurements and modifications of established liabilities.

descriptors.definition: When an entity uses the cost model, changes in decommissioning liabilities are added to or deducted from the asset's cost in the current period, adjusting the related provision. Any liability decrease exceeding the asset carrying amount is recognized immediately as income in the statement of profit and loss.
inclusion: Addition of liability increases to asset cost
Deduction of liability decreases from asset cost
Immediate profit and loss recognition for excess decreases
Impairment testing when additions raise asset carrying amounts
exclusion: Revaluation model adjustments
Changes unrelated to decommissioning or restoration obligations
nearby_distinctions: Differs from the revaluation model approach by directly adjusting asset cost rather than utilizing revaluation surplus reserves.

descriptors.definition: This appendix outlines the specific measurement events that alter existing decommissioning obligations, including revisions to estimated cash outflows, shifts in market-based discount rates, and time-value increments. It prescribes distinct accounting treatments for these changes based on whether the entity applies the cost model or the revaluation model.
inclusion: Changes in estimated resource outflows for settlement
Changes in current market-based discount rates
Increases reflecting the passage of time
exclusion: Initial estimations of site restoration costs
Operating expenses unrelated to asset retirement obligations
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on subsequent valuation triggers rather than general asset impairment triggers under Ind AS 36.

descriptors.definition: For assets measured under the revaluation model, increases in decommissioning liabilities are adjusted against revaluation surplus through other comprehensive income, while excess amounts are expensed. Decreases in these liabilities are similarly credited to the revaluation reserve, offsetting prior deficits and treating excesses as deemed revaluations.
inclusion: Liability increases offset against revaluation surplus
Liability decreases credited to revaluation reserve
Excess liability decreases treated as deemed revaluation in profit and loss
exclusion: Cost model asset adjustments
Standard routine operational maintenance costs
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from the cost model by running adjustments through revaluation reserves rather than directly modifying historical cost bases.

descriptors.definition: Entity disclosures reflect that property, plant, and equipment are stated at acquisition cost net of accumulated depreciation and impairment losses. Subsequent replacement costs are capitalized only when future economic benefits are probable, while routine repairs are expensed directly to profit or loss.
inclusion: Acquisition costs net of depreciation and impairment
Capitalized significant replacement and installation costs
Useful life schedules for various asset classes
exclusion: Routine maintenance and repair expenses
Unverified internal technical evaluations
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes capitalizable major component replacements from routine operational maintenance expensed in profit or loss.

descriptors.definition: Ind AS 16 excludes assets held for sale from its scope—deferring to Ind AS 105—and includes specific provisions for surface mine production stripping costs unlike older standards. Furthermore, it incorporates specific rules regarding net proceeds from testing items produced before an asset is available for use.
inclusion: Exclusion of non-current assets held for sale from Ind AS 16
Guidance on production phase stripping costs in surface mines
exclusion: Accounting standards for financial instruments
General revenue recognition principles
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts Ind AS 16 treatment of retired active-use assets against legacy AS 10 frameworks by routing held-for-sale assets through Ind AS 105.

descriptors.definition: Under Ind AS 16, net proceeds from selling items produced during testing are deducted from the cost of the property, plant, and equipment rather than credited to profit or loss. This treatment creates a carve-out from international standards, generating consequential impacts on subsequent depreciation, impairment, and deferred tax.
inclusion: Deduction of excess net proceeds from testing items against asset cost
Consequential impacts on depreciation and impairment
exclusion: Immediate profit or loss recognition of testing proceeds
Standard commercial revenue generation outside the testing phase
nearby_distinctions: Differs from IAS 16 by mandating cost reduction rather than profit or loss credit for proceeds generated during asset testing.

descriptors.definition: Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction, or production of a qualifying asset must be capitalized as part of that asset's cost. All other borrowing costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred.
inclusion: Directly attributable borrowing costs for qualifying assets
exclusion: Actual or imputed cost of equity
Preferred capital not classified as a liability
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes between mandatory capitalization for qualifying asset acquisition and expensing of general operational borrowing costs.

descriptors.definition: The standard governs the accounting treatment for borrowing costs but excludes the cost of equity and qualifying assets measured at fair value or repetitive inventories. It applies to interest expenses, lease liabilities, and qualifying foreign currency exchange differences.
inclusion: Interest expense using effective interest method
Interest on lease liabilities
Adjusted foreign currency exchange differences
exclusion: Actual or imputed cost of equity
Biological assets under fair value models
Inventories manufactured in large quantities repetitively
nearby_distinctions: Differentiates standard debt borrowing charges from equity issuance costs and fair-value measured assets.

descriptors.definition: Borrowing costs comprise interest, lease-related interest, and eligible exchange differences incurred on funds, while qualifying assets require a substantial period of time to get ready for use or sale. Short-term inventories and assets ready immediately upon acquisition are excluded from qualifying asset status.
inclusion: Manufacturing plants
Real estate and infrastructure assets
Power generation facilities
Intangible assets
exclusion: Short-term inventories
Financial assets
Assets ready for use or sale when acquired
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes long-term project assets needing extended preparation from short-term production inventories.

descriptors.definition: Foreign currency borrowing exchange losses are treated as eligible borrowing costs only up to the difference between the functional currency borrowing cost and the foreign currency borrowing cost. This adjustment represents the interest rate differential attributable to the foreign currency loan.
inclusion: Exchange losses equivalent to functional currency borrowing cost differential
exclusion: Exchange losses exceeding the functional currency interest rate differential
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes ordinary foreign exchange translation variances from structured interest-equivalent adjustments.

descriptors.definition: Directly attributable borrowing costs are capitalized when future economic benefits are probable and costs are measured reliably. For specific borrowings, eligible capitalization equals actual costs incurred less any investment income earned on temporary fund investments.
inclusion: Actual borrowing costs incurred on specific loans
Hyperinflationary adjustment exclusions
exclusion: Notional borrowing costs
Actual or imputed cost of equity
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts actual debt-financing charges with foregone earnings on internal equity resources.

descriptors.definition: Eligible borrowing costs are those that would have been avoided if asset expenditures had not been made. Specific borrowing calculations require deducting any investment income earned from temporarily deploying unspent specific loan funds.
inclusion: Actual borrowing costs net of temporary investment returns
exclusion: Notional interest on internal cash deployment
nearby_distinctions: Separates direct loan allocation mechanics from weighted-average general pool formulas.

descriptors.definition: General borrowing capitalization is determined by applying a weighted average capitalization rate of outstanding general loans to qualifying asset expenditures. Total capitalized amounts cannot exceed total borrowing costs incurred during the period.
inclusion: Weighted average borrowing costs of general debt pool
exclusion: Specific borrowings and their associated costs
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes pool-wide weighted interest rates from directly traceable specific loan interest.

descriptors.definition: Qualifying asset expenditures include cash payments, asset transfers, or interest-bearing liability assumptions, reduced by progress payments and government grants. The asset's average carrying amount during the period usually serves as the base for applying the capitalization rate.
inclusion: Cash expenditures
Transferred assets
Assumed interest-bearing liabilities
exclusion: Received progress payments
Associated government grants
nearby_distinctions: Separates gross outlay amounts from net capital expenditure bases adjusted for grants and progress billings.

descriptors.definition: When a qualifying asset's carrying amount or expected ultimate cost exceeds its recoverable amount or net realizable value, it must be written down or written off in accordance with applicable standards. Subsequent write-backs are permitted under specific conditions defined by those standards.
inclusion: Asset carrying value write-downs
Permissible write-backs
exclusion: Unadjusted carrying amounts exceeding asset value limits
nearby_distinctions: Differentiates standard cost capitalization caps from impairment-based asset valuation limits.

descriptors.definition: Capitalization of borrowing costs begins on the commencement date when expenditure, borrowing costs, and necessary preparation activities are all concurrently underway. Holding assets without active development does not qualify for capitalization.
inclusion: Technical and administrative work prior to physical construction
exclusion: Passive holding of land or assets without development
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes active pre-construction preparation from passive asset holding periods.

descriptors.definition: An entity must start capitalizing borrowing costs on the exact date it cumulatively incurs expenditures, incurs borrowing costs, and undertakes preparatory activities for the asset. Technical and administrative tasks like obtaining permits satisfy the preparatory activity requirement.
inclusion: Permit acquisition
Technical site planning
exclusion: Interest incurrence prior to expenditure or active development
nearby_distinctions: Differentiates isolated financial or physical milestones from the multi-condition cumulative commencement trigger.

descriptors.definition: Capitalization must be suspended during extended interruptions of active development but continues during normal temporary delays. It ceases entirely when substantially all activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete.
inclusion: Extended active development halts
Completion of physical construction
exclusion: Routine administrative work
Necessary temporary construction delays
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes extended interruption periods requiring cost suspension from standard temporary operational delays.

descriptors.definition: Capitalisation of borrowing costs must stop when substantially all activities required to prepare a qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are finished. Physical completion of construction normally signals this point even if minor administrative tasks or minor modifications remain outstanding.
inclusion: Borrowing costs incurred up to the date physical construction is complete
Partial completion where individual parts are capable of being used while construction continues on other parts
exclusion: Borrowing costs incurred after the asset is ready for its intended use or sale
Delays due to low occupancy or lack of rental uptake after physical completion
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from the commencement of capitalisation, which occurs when expenditure, borrowing costs, and asset preparation activities are all underway.

descriptors.definition: Entities are required to disclose the total amount of borrowing costs capitalised during the period alongside the specific capitalisation rate used. These disclosures ensure transparency regarding the financing costs added to the carrying value of qualifying assets.
inclusion: Amount of borrowing costs capitalised during the period
Capitalisation rate applied to determine eligible borrowing costs
exclusion: General operational expenses unrelated to asset capitalisation disclosures
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from recognition criteria and measurement mechanics of borrowing costs.

descriptors.definition: Specialized financing arrangements and group structures require targeted accounting treatment when determining eligible borrowing costs for capitalisation. These rules govern instruments classified as financial liabilities and loans originating from entities within a corporate group.
inclusion: Dividends on shares classified as financial liabilities
Borrowing cost capitalisation in group and separate financial statements
exclusion: Standard external bank borrowings lacking specific group or liability reclassification features
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from general standalone borrowing cost computations by addressing complex ownership or equity-liability boundary classifications.

descriptors.definition: Dividends payable on preference shares classified as financial liabilities under accounting standards meet the definition of borrowing costs. Consequently, such dividends can be capitalised if they fund the development of a qualifying asset following specific borrowing principles.
inclusion: Dividends on redeemable preference shares classified as financial liabilities
Capitalisation of qualifying dividend payments as interest
exclusion: Dividends on equity-classified instruments that do not meet liability definitions
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard equity distributions by their liability classification and treatment as finance expenses.

descriptors.definition: Group financial statements may capitalise interest on third-party borrowings held by one group entity even if the qualifying asset is developed by another. Such capitalisation is appropriate if the amount fairly reflects avoidable group interest costs, while separate financial statements rely on actual inter-company loan costs incurred.
inclusion: Group-level capitalisation reflecting third-party debt of a different group company
Borrowing costs on inter-company loans in separate financial statements of the subsidiary
exclusion: Capitalisation of third-party debt in the separate financial statements of an entity that holds no external borrowings
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from separate entity accounts where an entity lacking external borrowings cannot capitalise interest unless an actual inter-company loan exists.

descriptors.definition: Capitalisation of borrowing costs for maturing inventories continues as long as the inventory increases in value solely due to increasing age under a consistent business model. Once aging-related value appreciation cannot be demonstrated, inventories are treated as held for sale and capitalisation ceases.
inclusion: Addition of borrowing costs while items increase in value solely from aging
Inventories held to mature under a consistent business model
exclusion: Value increases driven by market fluctuations or general inflation
Inventories categorized strictly as held for sale
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from regular manufacturing production phases where completion of physical form ends production; maturing inventories accrue value over extended aging periods.

descriptors.definition: Practical reporting disclosures demonstrate how listed companies apply accounting standards to capitalise borrowing costs and define their underlying accounting policies. These disclosures specify the exact capitalisation rates utilized and the types of finance costs included.
inclusion: Disclosed amounts of borrowing costs capitalised into property, plant, and equipment
Applied capitalisation rates derived from annual financial statements
exclusion: General administrative costs and unallocated corporate overheads
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished as empirical illustrative reporting examples rather than standard-setting text mandates.

descriptors.definition: Significant structural variations exist between modern accounting standards and older frameworks regarding scope exclusions, measurement methods, and lease treatment. These differences affect how borrowing costs are calculated, scoped, and adjusted for foreign exchange variations.
terminology: Qualifying asset measured at fair value
inclusion: Scope exclusions for fair-value measured qualifying assets
Effective interest rate method calculations for borrowing costs
Inclusion of lease liabilities
exclusion: Legacy AS 16 treatment provisions that conflict with current Ind AS frameworks
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished by comparing contemporary Ind AS requirements directly against legacy AS guidelines to highlight operational framework divergences.

descriptors.definition: The standard prescribes methodologies to ensure assets are not carried above their recoverable amounts, requiring impairment loss recognition when carrying values exceed recoverable limits. It applies broadly to asset impairment accounting except for specifically exempted categories governed by other standards.
inclusion: property, plant, and equipment
intangible assets
goodwill
exclusion: inventories
deferred tax assets
financial assets under scope of Ind AS 109
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from other standards like Ind AS 2 which apply lower of cost and net realisable value measurements directly.

descriptors.definition: Key terms establish standard parameters for impairment testing, including carrying amounts, cash-generating units, corporate assets, and direct disposal costs. Depreciation and amortisation allocate depreciable amounts systematically across an asset's useful life.
inclusion: asset carrying value calculations
residual value deductions
depreciation allocations
exclusion: finance costs
income tax expense
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes incremental disposal costs from general financing and tax charges.

descriptors.definition: An impairment loss is recognized when an asset or cash-generating unit's carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, defined as the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. Entities must assess at each reporting period whether indicators suggest an asset may be impaired.
inclusion: fair value measurement parameters
discounted future cash flow calculations
period-end impairment evaluations
exclusion: carrying value adjustments without test triggers
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes fair value less costs of disposal from value in use as components of recoverable amount.

descriptors.definition: Entities must evaluate internal and external sources of information at each reporting date to identify potential asset impairment. Specific assets require mandatory annual impairment testing regardless of whether indicators are present.
inclusion: declines in market value
adverse technological or economic environment changes
physical damage evidence
exclusion: temporary market fluctuations without adverse operational impact
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes general assets requiring conditional indicator tests from specific assets mandated for annual reviews.

descriptors.definition: An asset is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, prompting an estimate of the recoverable amount. Entities evaluate reporting period indicators to determine if detailed impairment calculations are necessary.
inclusion: period-end indicator assessments
recoverable amount estimations
exclusion: assets exempted from standard scope
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes baseline periodic indicator reviews from mandatory annual reviews for special asset classes.

descriptors.definition: Assessment criteria include external market shifts, technological changes, and interest rate movements alongside internal evidence of physical damage, obsolescence, or underperformance. These indicators dictate when an entity must calculate an asset's recoverable amount.
inclusion: market value drops
idle assets
higher than budgeted operating costs
exclusion: normal wear and tear within expected parameters
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes macroeconomic external market indicators from microeconomic entity-specific internal operational evidence.

descriptors.definition: Specific asset classes require annual impairment testing regardless of whether impairment indicators exist. These reviews must follow consistent annual timing, supplemented by additional testing if interim impairment indicators arise.
inclusion: intangible assets with indefinite useful lives
intangible assets not yet available for use
goodwill acquired in business combinations
exclusion: finite-lived tangible and intangible assets without impairment indicators
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes mandatory scheduled annual testing from event-driven contingent impairment testing.

descriptors.definition: Certain high-risk assets bypass indicator checks and must be tested for impairment annually. This ensures potential value erosion in unamortized or unproven assets is captured proactively.
inclusion: goodwill
indefinite life intangibles
development-stage intangibles
exclusion: standard depreciable plant and equipment
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes assets requiring automatic annual tests from assets requiring triggering indicators.

descriptors.definition: Intangibles with indefinite useful lives or those not yet ready for use must be tested annually and whenever indicators suggest possible impairment. Previous detailed recoverable amount calculations may be reused under strict criteria if prior margins were substantial and asset configurations remain unchanged.
inclusion: consistent annual timing windows
prior period calculation carryforwards under specific conditions
exclusion: intangibles with material changes in underlying cash-generating units
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes strict mandatory annual timing rules from conditional use of prior-period calculations.

descriptors.definition: Cash-generating units allocated with goodwill must be tested for impairment annually by comparing the aggregate unit carrying amount with its recoverable amount. Individual assets or smaller constituent units showing impairment signs must be tested before evaluating the wider cash-generating unit or goodwill group.
inclusion: annual goodwill impairment reviews
hierarchical asset testing sequences
exclusion: goodwill tested in isolation without unit allocation
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes testing of individual constituent assets within a unit prior to testing the overarching goodwill cash-generating unit.

descriptors.definition: An asset or cash-generating unit's recoverable amount is determined as the higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use. Calculating both metrics is unnecessary if either value alone exceeds the asset carrying amount, confirming no impairment exists.
terminology: fair value less costs of disposal
inclusion: fair value metrics
value in use cash flow models
single-metric shortcut tests
exclusion: mandatory dual-metric calculation when carrying amount is safely exceeded
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes standalone individual asset testing from cash-generating unit testing when independent cash flows are absent.

descriptors.definition: Recoverable amounts are assessed for individual assets unless they lack independent cash inflows, requiring evaluation at the cash-generating unit level. Measurement requires comparing carrying values against the higher of fair value less costs of disposal or value in use.
inclusion: cash-generating unit aggregation
higher of fair value or value in use tests
exclusion: isolated asset evaluations where independent cash streams do not exist
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes individual asset testing scope from broader cash-generating unit testing scope.

descriptors.definition: An entity is excused from calculating both fair value less costs of disposal and value in use if either metric alone exceeds the asset carrying amount. Furthermore, if fair value less costs of disposal cannot be reliably estimated, the recoverable amount is based entirely on value in use.
terminology: Fair value less costs of disposal
inclusion: Using one recoverable amount measure if it exceeds carrying value
Relying solely on value in use when fair value cannot be estimated
exclusion: Calculating both metrics when neither individually exceeds the carrying amount
nearby_distinctions: Differs from general dual calculation rules by applying shortcuts or single-metric reliance under specific conditions.

descriptors.definition: Recoverable amounts are assessed for cash-generating units when individual assets fail to generate largely independent cash inflows. However, individual asset testing remains sufficient if its fair value exceeds carrying value or if both measurement bases are closely aligned.
terminology: Fair value less costs of disposal
inclusion: Determining recoverable amount at the cash-generating unit level
Individual asset testing when fair value exceeds carrying amount
exclusion: Assessing cash-generating units when individual assets have clearly independent cash flows
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes standalone asset impairment testing from group-level cash-generating unit evaluations.

descriptors.definition: Fair value less costs of disposal is determined by taking the price received to sell an asset in an orderly market transaction and deducting incremental direct disposal costs. Finance costs and income taxes are strictly excluded from these deductible disposal expenses.
inclusion: Incremental costs directly attributable to asset disposal
Prices established in orderly market transactions
exclusion: Finance costs
Income tax expense
nearby_distinctions: Differs from value in use by relying on market participant assumptions rather than entity-specific expectations.

descriptors.definition: Fair value represents the exit price between market participants on the measurement date following specific valuation standards. Costs of disposal cover direct incremental expenses incurred to sell an asset, excluding general business reorganization costs.
inclusion: Direct incremental disposal expenditures
Market-based transaction prices
exclusion: Termination benefits
Business reorganization expenses following disposal
nearby_distinctions: Separates direct transaction costs from post-disposal operational restructuring expenses.

descriptors.definition: Direct incremental expenses required to make an asset ready for sale, such as legal fees and stamp duty, are deducted to find fair value less costs of disposal. Liabilities already recognized for these items are handled separately to avoid double-counting.
inclusion: Stamp duty and transaction taxes
Asset removal and preparation costs
exclusion: Termination benefits under Ind AS 19
Business reduction or reorganization costs
nearby_distinctions: Differentiates between direct sale-preparation costs and subsequent internal restructuring overheads.

descriptors.definition: Fair value incorporates generalized market participant assumptions, whereas value in use incorporates entity-specific factors. Consequently, fair value excludes private synergies, asset-grouping premiums, and owner-specific legal or tax privileges.
inclusion: General market pricing assumptions
Universal market parameters
exclusion: Owner-specific legal rights or restrictions
Proprietary asset grouping values and internal synergies
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts external market consensus valuation with internal cash-flow-based utility assessments.

descriptors.definition: Value in use is computed as the present value of estimated future cash flows derived from an asset or cash-generating unit. The computation factors in the time value of money, inherent uncertainty risks, and cash flow variations.
inclusion: Estimated future cash inflows and outflows
Market risk-free rates and uncertainty pricing
exclusion: Financing cash flows
Income tax receipts or payments
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes entity-specific operational utility valuations from open-market exchange prices.

descriptors.definition: Value in use measures the present value of expected cash flows generated through continuous utilization and ultimate disposal. It accounts for cash flow variations and risks through weighted averages of possible outcomes.
inclusion: Cash inflows and outflows from asset utilization
Disposal proceeds at the end of useful life
exclusion: Future reorganizations uncommitted by management
Asset performance enhancements
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on internal operational generation rather than immediate market liquidation value.

descriptors.definition: Cash flow projections must rely on reasonable, supportable assumptions reflecting management's best estimates over the remaining useful life, prioritizing external evidence. Projections utilize approved management budgets while excluding uncommitted future enhancements or restructurings.
inclusion: Management's best estimate assumptions
Most recent approved financial budgets
exclusion: Uncommitted future restructuring cash flows
Enhancements improving future asset performance beyond current state
nearby_distinctions: Isolates baseline operational performance from speculative future capital expansions.

descriptors.definition: The discount rate used for value in use must be a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessments of the time value of money and asset-specific risks. It should exclude risks already factored into the future cash flow estimates to avoid double counting.
inclusion: Current market assessments of time value of money
Asset-specific risk adjustments not already in cash flows
exclusion: Risks already accounted for in cash flow projections
Entity capital structure distortions independent of the asset
nearby_distinctions: Separates asset-specific return requirements from general corporate financing cost structures.

descriptors.definition: An impairment loss is recognized immediately in profit or loss when an asset carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount. For revalued assets, the loss is treated as a revaluation decrease against equity surplus rather than profit or loss.
inclusion: Immediate profit or loss recognition for cost-model assets
Offsetting revaluation surplus for revalued assets
exclusion: Treating revalued asset impairments as standard profit or loss expenses when surplus exists
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes accounting treatment for assets held under historical cost versus revaluation models.

descriptors.definition: When an individual asset carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, it is written down via an impairment loss. Subsequent depreciation must be adjusted to allocate the revised carrying amount systematically over the remaining useful life.
inclusion: Carrying amount write-downs
Systematic future depreciation adjustments
exclusion: Maintaining unadjusted depreciation schedules after write-downs
nearby_distinctions: Links current-period impairment adjustments directly to future periods depreciation allocations.

descriptors.definition: A cash-generating unit represents the smallest identifiable group of assets that generates largely independent cash inflows. When an individual asset lacks an independent recoverable amount, the entity determines the recoverable amount of the broader asset group to which it belongs.
inclusion: Entire entities
Business units or departments
Production lines
Groups of property, plant, and equipment
exclusion: Individual assets whose recoverable amounts can be determined independently
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from individual assets because it aggregates multiple asset items to isolate independent cash streams.

descriptors.definition: When goodwill cannot be allocated on a non-arbitrary basis to individual units, the separate units must be tested for impairment before evaluating the broader group containing the associated goodwill. This ensures proper sequencing when assessing impairment for units sharing unallocated goodwill.
inclusion: Goodwill allocated to groups of cash-generating units
exclusion: Goodwill that can be directly allocated to individual units on a non-arbitrary basis
nearby_distinctions: Differs from single CGU testing by requiring a sequential two-tier approach when goodwill serves multiple units.

descriptors.definition: Entities must assess at each reporting period whether prior impairment losses for assets other than goodwill have decreased or no longer exist. Reversals occur exclusively when changes in the estimates used to determine the recoverable amount happen since the last loss was recognized.
inclusion: Assets other than goodwill showing indicators of impairment reversal
exclusion: Goodwill impairment losses
Increases in carrying amount purely due to the passage of time
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from time-based discount unwinding, which does not reflect increased asset service potential.

descriptors.definition: An entity must evaluate at each reporting date if prior impairment losses on non-goodwill assets have reversed due to altered estimation parameters. Such reversals reflect an increase in the estimated service potential of the asset from either use or sale.
inclusion: Prior period impairment losses on non-goodwill assets
exclusion: Goodwill impairment reversals
Passage of time value increases
nearby_distinctions: Differs from initial impairment testing by focusing on positive changes in service potential rather than adverse declines.

descriptors.definition: Entities identify potential impairment reversals by monitoring external and internal indicators such as significant increases in asset value, technological enhancements, or improved economic performance. The presence of these triggers requires estimating the asset's current recoverable amount.
inclusion: Significant asset value increases
Favorable market or technological environment changes
Decreased market interest rates
Internal evidence of superior economic performance
exclusion: Routine market fluctuations without substantive impact on service potential
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from impairment indicators by focusing on positive operational or economic enhancements rather than adverse declines.

descriptors.definition: The increased carrying amount of an asset from an impairment reversal is capped at the historical carrying amount net of depreciation that would have existed had no impairment occurred. Reversals are generally recognized directly in profit or loss unless the asset is carried at a revalued amount.
inclusion: Individual non-goodwill assets
Revalued assets treated under relevant valuation standards
exclusion: Goodwill
Excess increases treated as revaluations
nearby_distinctions: Differs from revaluation surplus accounting by being limited strictly to the pre-impairment depreciated historical cost baseline.

descriptors.definition: Impairment reversals for a cash-generating unit are allocated pro rata across the unit's assets, excluding goodwill, based on their carrying amounts. Individual asset increases are capped at the lower of their recoverable amount or their hypothetical depreciated historical carrying amount.
inclusion: Assets within a cash-generating unit excluding goodwill
exclusion: Goodwill
nearby_distinctions: Differs from individual asset reversal by requiring proportional allocation across multiple assets subject to individual asset caps.

descriptors.definition: Impairment losses recognized for goodwill in prior periods cannot be reversed under any subsequent circumstances. Any subsequent increase in goodwill value reflects internally generated goodwill rather than a reversal of acquired goodwill.
inclusion: Previously recognized goodwill impairment losses
exclusion: Impairment reversals for tangible or identifiable intangible assets
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from other assets because goodwill cannot absorb reversals due to prohibitions against recognizing internal goodwill.

descriptors.definition: When non-controlling interest is measured at its proportionate share of net identifiable assets rather than fair value, unrecognised NCI goodwill must be grossed up for impairment testing. This grossed-up carrying amount is compared against the recoverable amount of the unit.
inclusion: Subsidiaries with non-controlling interests measured at proportionate net identifiable assets
exclusion: Subsidiaries where non-controlling interest is measured at acquisition-date fair value
nearby_distinctions: Differs from full fair value NCI methods by requiring an explicit adjustment to incorporate unrecognised NCI goodwill before testing.

descriptors.definition: Entities must disclose financial statement line items, amounts, and comprehensive details regarding impairment losses and reversals across asset classes and segments. These disclosures provide transparency regarding the financial impact of asset impairments.
inclusion: Impairment losses and reversals recognised in profit or loss
Impairment losses and reversals recognised in other comprehensive income
exclusion: General operational depreciation and amortisation expenses
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard depreciation disclosures by focusing explicitly on abnormal downward revaluations and recoveries.

descriptors.definition: Entities are required to disclose class-specific impairment losses and reversals recognized in profit or loss and other comprehensive income during the reporting period. This information may be integrated within standard asset class reconciliations such as property, plant, and equipment schedules.
inclusion: Impairment losses and reversals by asset class
exclusion: Segment-specific reporting disclosures handled separately
nearby_distinctions: Differs from material event disclosures by focusing on aggregated class-level totals rather than specific individual loss events.

descriptors.definition: Entities reporting segment information under Ind AS 108 must disclose impairment losses and reversals recognized in both profit or loss and other comprehensive income for each reportable segment. This ensures visibility of impairment trends across business segments.
inclusion: Segment-level impairment losses
Segment-level impairment reversals
exclusion: Unallocated corporate asset impairments lacking segment attribution
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from entity-wide class disclosures by segregating financial figures strictly according to reportable operating segments.

descriptors.definition: An entity must disclose specific details for each material impairment loss or reversal recognized during the period for individual assets or cash-generating units. Required disclosures include underlying events, financial amounts, asset classification, and fair value hierarchy levels or valuation techniques.
inclusion: events leading to recognition or reversal
amount of impairment loss or reversal
nature and segment of individual assets
description and class breakdown of cash-generating units
valuation hierarchy levels and key assumptions for fair value less costs of disposal
exclusion: immaterial aggregate impairment losses
general unallocated corporate assets lacking specific impairment events
nearby_distinctions: Unlike aggregate disclosures for minor losses, this node mandates granular reporting for individually material impairment events.

descriptors.definition: When individual impairment losses or reversals are not material on a standalone basis, an entity must disclose aggregate figures if they are material collectively. This includes identifying the primary asset classes affected and the principal economic events driving these aggregate adjustments.
inclusion: aggregate impairment losses for the period
aggregate impairment reversals for the period
main classes of affected assets
main events and circumstances causing the losses and reversals
exclusion: material individual impairment losses reported separately
immaterial items not qualifying as material in aggregate
nearby_distinctions: Distinct from itemized disclosures of material individual losses by focusing strictly on pooled figures that become significant only when combined.

descriptors.definition: If a portion of goodwill acquired in a business combination remains unallocated to any cash-generating unit at the end of the reporting period, the entity must disclose that specific amount. Additionally, the entity is required to provide clear reasons explaining why the goodwill allocation has not yet been completed.
inclusion: monetary amount of unallocated goodwill at period end
justifications explaining why the goodwill amount remains unallocated
exclusion: goodwill successfully allocated to specific cash-generating units or groups of units
nearby_distinctions: Differs from allocated goodwill disclosures because it addresses acquisition synergies that have not yet been successfully assigned to operating cash-generating units.

descriptors.definition: Entities holding cash-generating units with significant allocations of goodwill or indefinite-life intangibles must disclose detailed valuation inputs. This includes the basis of recoverable amount determination, growth rates, projection periods, and applied discount rates.
inclusion: carrying amount of allocated goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles
basis of recoverable amount determination
management's key assumptions and projection approaches
forecast periods exceeding five years with justifications
growth rates and discount rates applied to cash flows
exclusion: cash-generating units where goodwill or indefinite-life intangibles are insignificant in comparison to total carrying amounts
nearby_distinctions: Applies strictly to units with significant carrying amounts of goodwill or indefinite-life intangibles, separating them from minor allocations.

descriptors.definition: When goodwill or indefinite-life intangibles are allocated across multiple units where each allocation is insignificant individually but significant in aggregate, specific disclosures are required. Entities must disclose the aggregate carrying amounts, shared key assumptions, and sensitivity details if reasonably possible changes would eliminate the headroom.
inclusion: aggregate carrying amounts of insignificant allocations
description of shared key assumptions and management approaches
excess of recoverable amount over carrying amount when sensitive
required change in key assumptions to trigger impairment
exclusion: individually significant goodwill or indefinite-life intangible allocations
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on pooled insignificant units that share common key assumptions, contrasting with standalone reporting for individually large units.

descriptors.definition: This section provides practical illustrations and comparative standard overviews regarding impairment accounting policies applied by listed entities. It serves as a structural transition into comparing Indian Accounting Standards with predecessor accounting rules.
inclusion: annual report references for impairment policies
comparative framework tables highlighting differences between Ind AS and AS
exclusion: hypothetical numerical exercises not drawn from actual financial statements
nearby_distinctions: Acts as an empirical application guide preceding technical standard comparisons rather than containing isolated theoretical rules.

descriptors.definition: This comparative framework details the structural and technical divergences between Ind AS 36 and AS 28 regarding asset scope, annual testing rules, and goodwill reversals. Major differences include mandatory annual testing for goodwill under Ind AS and differing treatments for goodwill impairment reversals.
inclusion: inclusion of specific financial assets and exclusion of biological assets under Ind AS 36
mandatory annual impairment testing for indefinite-life intangibles and goodwill
prohibition of goodwill impairment reversals under Ind AS 36 versus allowance under AS 28
differences in bottom-up and top-down allocation approaches
exclusion: harmonized rules where Ind AS 36 and AS 28 maintain identical provisions without divergence
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts modern global convergence accounting treatments with legacy local accounting standards for asset impairment.

descriptors.definition: This standard prescribes the accounting treatment for intangible assets that are not specifically addressed within another standard. It mandates criteria for recognition, measurement, and disclosure, requiring initial measurement at cost and subsequent measurement at either cost or revaluation model.
inclusion: Intangible assets not specifically covered under other standards
exclusion: Intangible assets held for sale in ordinary course of business
Deferred tax assets
Financial assets
Goodwill arising in business combinations
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from other standards like Ind AS 2, Ind AS 12, and Ind AS 103 which govern specific asset categories.

descriptors.definition: The standard applies to all intangible assets except those explicitly scoped out, such as financial assets, exploration and evaluation assets, and mineral extraction expenditures. Items incorporating both tangible and intangible elements require professional judgment to determine the more significant component.
inclusion: Computer software not integral to hardware
Licences and patents
exclusion: Financial assets under Ind AS 32
Exploration and evaluation assets under Ind AS 106
Mineral development and extraction expenditures
nearby_distinctions: Distinguishes between standalone intangible software and software that is an integral part of hardware governed by Ind AS 16.

descriptors.definition: The standard applies to all intangible assets except those governed by other specific standards or specific excluded categories like mineral extraction expenditures. Entities evaluate items containing both physical and intangible elements by assessing which component is more significant.
